milestones.title: Portuguese traders reach the lagoon
milestones.detail: Portuguese ships began trading in the lagoon around 1472. Awori Yoruba fishing and farming communities already lived on the islands, under the Olofin of Iddo.
milestones.source: Kristin Mann (2007), Slavery and the Birth of an African City: Lagos, 1760-1900, pp. 24-26, via https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_Lagos

milestones.title: Benin makes Lagos Island a military post (Eko)
milestones.detail: Around 1600 the Kingdom of Benin took control and Lagos Island became a fortified Benin camp. Ashipa was appointed ruler and founded the dynasty of the Obas of Lagos, who paid tribute to Benin until 1830.
milestones.source: Mann (2007), pp. 27-29, and S. A. Akintoye (2014), A History of the Yoruba People, p. 235, via https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_Lagos

milestones.title: Lagos opens to the Atlantic slave trade
milestones.detail: Oba Akinsemoyin, who took the throne in the 1760s, opened the town to European slave traders. The trade grew fast in the 1780s and made Lagos a leading slave port of the Bight of Benin.

milestones.title: British bombardment of Lagos
milestones.detail: A Royal Navy squadron attacked the town, removed Oba Kosoko and restored Akitoye, who signed a treaty abolishing the slave trade on 1 January 1852. A British consulate followed.
milestones.source: Robert S. Smith (1979), The Lagos Consulate 1851-1861, via https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timeline_of_Lagos

milestones.title: Lagos ceded to Britain
milestones.detail: Oba Dosunmu signed the Lagos Treaty of Cession on 6 August 1861 under threat of bombardment. Lagos was declared a British colony on 5 March 1862.
milestones.source: Smith (1979), The Lagos Consulate 1851-1861, p. 121, via https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_Lagos

milestones.title: Electric lighting switched on
milestones.detail: Electricity supply began on 19 September 1898 with 60 kW of generation, lighting the Marina from Government House to the north side of the island.
milestones.source: Ayodeji Olukoju (2003), Infrastructure Development and Urban Facilities in Lagos, 1861-2000, chapter 2, via https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_Lagos

milestones.title: Railway to Ibadan and Carter Bridge open
milestones.detail: The Lagos Government Railway to Ibadan, begun in 1896, opened on 4 March 1901. In the same year Carter Bridge gave Lagos Island its first fixed link to the mainland.
milestones.source: https://railwaywondersoftheworld.com/nigeria.html (railway) and R. Oyelaran-Oyeyinka, Governance and Bureaucracy: Leadership in Nigeria's Public Service (Carter Bridge), both via https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_Lagos

milestones.title: Capital of a unified Nigeria
milestones.detail: Northern and Southern Nigeria were merged on 1 January 1914 into the Colony and Protectorate of Nigeria, with Lagos as its capital.
milestones.source: Statesman's Year-Book (1921), 'British Empire: West Africa: Nigeria', via https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timeline_of_Lagos

milestones.title: Bubonic plague and clearance of the island
milestones.detail: Plague broke out in 1924 and lasted until 1931, with 1,947 recorded cases. Swamps were drained and crowded quarters on Lagos Island were cleared, with residents resettled on the mainland.
milestones.source: O. A. Faleye (2019), Gesnerus, and Olukoju (2003), https://books.openedition.org/ifra/828, via https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_Lagos

milestones.title: Independence proclaimed at the racecourse
milestones.detail: Nigerian independence was proclaimed in 1960 at the Lagos racecourse, now Tafawa Balewa Square. Lagos stayed the federal capital.

milestones.title: Lagos State created
milestones.detail: The new state joined the old municipality to the mainland districts that the city had already grown into, such as Mushin, Ikeja and Agege.
milestones.source: UN-HABITAT (2004), State of the World's Cities 2004/2005, via https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timeline_of_Lagos

milestones.title: FESTAC 77 held in Lagos
milestones.detail: The Second World Black and African Festival of Arts and Culture was held in 1977. The National Theatre at Iganmu, finished in 1976, and the Festac Town housing estate were built for it.
milestones.source: Toyin Falola & Ann Genova (2009), Historical Dictionary of Nigeria, via https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timeline_of_Lagos

milestones.title: Third Mainland Bridge opens
milestones.detail: The 11.8 km bridge across the lagoon, the longest of the three links between Lagos Island and the mainland, opened in 1990.

milestones.title: Federal capital moves to Abuja
milestones.detail: The seat of the federal government officially moved from Lagos to Abuja on 12 December 1991. Lagos remained the country's commercial centre.
milestones.source: Falola & Genova (2009), Historical Dictionary of Nigeria, 'Chronology', via https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lagos

milestones.title: Bus rapid transit begins
milestones.detail: The Lagos Bus Rapid Transit system was inaugurated in 2008, with dedicated bus lanes on Ikorodu Road.

milestones.title: Blue Line urban rail opens
milestones.detail: The Lagos light rail system began operating in 2023 with the Blue Line between Mile 2 and Marina. The Red Line followed in 2024.

notes: Start date: there is no documented founding. Awori Yoruba tradition (the Olofin and his sons) is undated; historians place Awori settlement on the islands by the 15th century and Portuguese contact with the lagoon around 1472, and the Benin military camp (Eko) around 1600. 1472 is used as the earliest externally anchored date and marked 'estimated'; the date is contested and some accounts say Lagos was founded in the 16th century. Population: nothing before 1789, and the four figures for 1789-1861 are rough estimates listed without discussion in Akinyoade et al. (2017). Colonial censuses run from 1866; the 1866-1901 counts cover the town on Lagos Island only, 1911 onward the enlarged township (18 square miles in 1911, 24.24 in 1931), so the series is not like-for-like. Published tables disagree by a few hundred on several censuses (1901: 41,487 / 41,847 / 38,387; 1921: 98,303 / 99,690; 1931: 126,474 / 126,108); Olukoju (2003) is followed, and Fourchard notes that all these counts were house-to-house estimates that undercount. The 1891 figure was found only rounded. No 1940s count was found (the next census was 1950). Landmarks: only six had a sourced height. Left out for lack of a sourced height: Iga Idunganran palace, Shitta-Bey Mosque (1892), Cathedral Church of Christ (1946), Holy Cross Cathedral (1939), Lagos Central Mosque (1988), Tafawa Balewa Square, National Stadium, Carter Bridge and Third Mainland Bridge. The Lekki-Ikoyi Link Bridge (2013) was left out because sources give its pylon as 50 m, 90 m or 91 m. Civic Centre Tower was left out because CTBUH (75 m, estimated) and other sources (90 m) disagree. Landmark coordinates are from Wikipedia.
